Q: SQL to Excel comparison A:

The issue is that LEFT() turns the date into text, while the other Excel cell contains a real date value. They look the same, but Excel sees them as different.

Use:

=DATEVALUE(LEFT(A1,9))

This converts the SQL date text into a real Excel date, so the comparison should work.

Q: How to improve contour detection of holes in white wall A:

Here is one way to do that in Python/OpenCV

  • Read the input

  • Convert to grayscale

  • Threshold

  • Invert the threshold so holes are white on black background

  • Get contours

  • Draw contours on copy of input if large enough

  • Save results

Input:



import cv2
import numpy as np

# read the input
img = cv2.imread("wall_holes.jpg")

# convert to grayscale
gray = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)

# threshold
thresh = cv2.threshold(gray, 100, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY)[1]

# invert
thresh2 = 255 - thresh

# get contours
contours = cv2.findContours(thresh2, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
contours = contours[0] if len(contours) == 2 else contours[1]

# draw contours on copy of input
result = np.copy(img)
for cntr in contours:
    area = cv2.contourArea(cntr)
    if area > 50:
        cv2.drawContours(result, [cntr], 0, (0,0,255), 2)

# save results
cv2.imwrite("wall_holes_gray.jpg", gray)
cv2.imwrite("wall_holes_thresh.png", thresh)
cv2.imwrite("wall_holes_result.png", result)

# show results
cv2.imshow('input',img)
cv2.imshow('gray', gray)
cv2.imshow('thresh', thresh)
cv2.imshow('result', result)
cv2.waitKey(0)

Q: Set up analytic infrastructure A:

A common approach is:

Application databases → ETL/ELT pipeline → Reporting database or data warehouse → Dashboard

Do not normally run dashboard queries directly on production databases. Large reporting queries may slow down the applications.

Use an ETL or ELT process to copy data from each application into one central reporting system. For a small project, PostgreSQL may be enough. For larger systems, you can use BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift or Microsoft Fabric.

Store the data in simple layers:

  • Raw data: copied from the source databases.

  • Clean data: corrected and standardised.

  • Reporting data: prepared tables and aggregates for dashboards.

Tools such as Airbyte or Fivetran can move the data. SQL or dbt can clean and transform it. Power BI, Tableau, Metabase or Superset can create the dashboards.

Also include a customer or tenant_id field and use access controls so each user only sees their own data.

Start with one application and one dashboard. Add more data sources after the first pipeline works reliably.

Q: Extracting HDR surfaces from ggdensity to plot them with ggplot A:

so

geom_hdr() ultimately draws isoband polygons, but the cleanest way to calculate their surfaces is to call the underlying ggdensity::get_hdr() function for each category.

Because the regions are nested, the area of the (p)-HDR can be approximated by summing the areas of the grid cells belonging to that HDR.

library(ggplot2)
library(ggdensity)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(tibble)

probs <- c(0.50, 0.80, 0.95, 0.99)
n_grid <- 400

# Use identical limits for every subgroup
x_range <- range(DF$Longitude)
y_range <- range(DF$Latitude)

hdr_surfaces <- DF |>
  split(DF$Category) |>
  imap_dfr(function(dat, category) {

    hdr <- get_hdr(
      data = data.frame(
        x = dat$Longitude,
        y = dat$Latitude
      ),
      method = "kde",
      probs = probs,
      n = n_grid,
      rangex = x_range,
      rangey = y_range,
      hdr_membership = FALSE
    )

    grid <- hdr$df_est

    # Surface represented by one grid cell
    dx <- median(diff(sort(unique(grid$x))))
    dy <- median(diff(sort(unique(grid$y))))
    cell_surface <- dx * dy

    map_dfr(probs, function(p) {
      tibble(
        Category = category,
        probability = p,
        surface = sum(grid$hdr <= p, na.rm = TRUE) *
          cell_surface
      )
    })
  })

hdr_surfaces

The resulting surface is expressed in square coordinate units, which in this example means square degrees.

The surfaces can then be displayed using geom_col():

ggplot(
  hdr_surfaces,
  aes(
    x = factor(probability, levels = probs),
    y = surface,
    fill = Category
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
    width = 0.7
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(
    labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "HDR probability",
    y = expression("HDR surface (" * degree^2 * ")"),
    fill = "Category"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

To ensure that the calculated HDRs and the displayed HDRs use the same settings, explicitly use the same probabilities, grid size and coordinate limits in geom_hdr():

DF_Plot <- ggplot(
  DF,
  aes(
    x = Longitude,
    y = Latitude,
    fill = Category
  )
) +
  geom_hdr(
    probs = probs,
    n = n_grid,
    xlim = x_range,
    ylim = y_range
  ) +
  coord_equal()

DF_Plot

Since the coordinates represent longitude and latitude, square degrees are generally not an appropriate geographic area unit.

A better approach is to project the data into a metric coordinate reference system before estimating the HDRs. For these coordinates, UTM zone 28N, EPSG:32628, is a suitable projected coordinate system.

library(sf)

DF_projected <- st_as_sf(
  DF,
  coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"),
  crs = 4326
) |>
  st_transform(32628)

xy <- st_coordinates(DF_projected)

DF_metric <- DF_projected |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(
    x = xy[, "X"],
    y = xy[, "Y"]
  )

Calculate the HDR surfaces using the projected coordinates:

x_range_m <- range(DF_metric$x)
y_range_m <- range(DF_metric$y)

hdr_surfaces_km2 <- DF_metric |>
  split(DF_metric$Category) |>
  imap_dfr(function(dat, category) {

    hdr <- get_hdr(
      data = data.frame(
        x = dat$x,
        y = dat$y
      ),
      method = "kde",
      probs = probs,
      n = n_grid,
      rangex = x_range_m,
      rangey = y_range_m,
      hdr_membership = FALSE
    )

    grid <- hdr$df_est

    dx <- median(diff(sort(unique(grid$x))))
    dy <- median(diff(sort(unique(grid$y))))
    cell_surface_m2 <- dx * dy

    map_dfr(probs, function(p) {
      tibble(
        Category = category,
        probability = p,
        surface_km2 =
          sum(grid$hdr <= p, na.rm = TRUE) *
          cell_surface_m2 / 1e6
      )
    })
  })

hdr_surfaces_km2

Plot the surfaces in square kilometres:

ggplot(
  hdr_surfaces_km2,
  aes(
    x = factor(probability, levels = probs),
    y = surface_km2,
    fill = Category
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
    width = 0.7
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(
    labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "HDR probability",
    y = expression("HDR surface (km"^2 * ")"),
    fill = "Category"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Increasing n_grid improves the numerical approximation of the surface, although it also increases computation time. A value between approximately 300 and 500 is generally more suitable for estimating areas than a coarse grid.

Q: How to INSERT a string that is similar to a JSON structure A:

JSON validity

The original sample string is not a properly formed JSON string. For JSON, each property name must be enclosed in a pair of double quotes "...", and the value to a property cannot be empty.

I'd suggest the original string should be corrected as the following:

[ {"Pallet": 1, "Loaded": null, "LoadedTimestamp": null },
  {"Pallet": 2, "Loaded": "True", "LoadedTimestamp": "2026-07-27 12:00 AM"} ]'

T‑SQL Implementation

To extract JSON string into SQL table is achievable with a single INSERT ... SELECT ... FROM OPENJSON ... WITH ... statement. There's no need to use a loop. For testing purpose, a test table DstTable is created with each row using the same property names from the JSON record as column names in table row. However, there is no requirement you must use the same names.

-- drop the test table for regression test
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS DstTable;

-- test data
DECLARE @source NVARCHAR(MAX) =
N'[ {"Pallet": 1, "Loaded": null, "LoadedTimestamp": null },
    {"Pallet": 2, "Loaded": "True", "LoadedTimestamp": "2026-07-27 12:00 AM"} ]';

-- test table, simulate each record in JSON data array
CREATE TABLE DstTable(
    Pallet INT,
    Loaded BIT,
    LoadedTimestamp DATETIME,
);

-- actual statement to extract JSON into table
INSERT DstTable(Pallet, Loaded, LoadedTimestamp)
SELECT Pallet, IIF(Loaded = 'True', 1, 0), LoadedTimestamp
FROM OPENJSON(@source)
WITH (
    Pallet INT '$.Pallet',
    Loaded NVARCHAR(5) '$.Loaded',
    LoadedTimestamp DATETIME '$.LoadedTimestamp'
);

-- show result
SELECT Pallet, Loaded, LoadedTimestamp
FROM DstTable;

The following is the text output on SSMS:

(2 rows affected)
Pallet      Loaded LoadedTimestamp
----------- ------ -----------------------
1           0      NULL
2           1      2026-07-27 00:00:00.000

(2 rows affected)


Completion time: 2026-07-27T23:09:43.6332377+08:00

Reference

OPENJSON (Transact-SQL)

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/functions/openjson-transact-sql

Q: How to use CONVERT() in a CodeIgniter order_by() query builder method call without corrupting the rendered SQL A:

At least in CodeIgniter 3, auto-escaping can be disabled via the 3rd parameter of the order_by() method call. This allows you to pass in a string with your own custom quoting.

$this->db->order_by(
    sprintf(
        'CONVERT(%s, SIGNED)',
        $this->db->escape_identifiers('codExtern')
    ),
    ''
    false
);

See also: ORDER BY clause to sort values in an explicit order in CodeIgniter

That said, when I tested your ORDER BY condition in CodeIgniter3.1.13, with a column name that doesn't actually need quoting, the SQL was rendered without any quotes (valid SQL) because of the existence of a parenthesis in the first parameter. So unless you've used a reserved keyword or unfriendly characters in your column name, just do this:

$this->db->order_by('CONVERT(column_name, SIGNED)');

Renders:

ORDER BY CONVERT(column_name, SIGNED)

This is the same reason that $this->db->order_by('RAND(column_name)'); works without explicitly disabling escaping.
...but if you need that, CI natively affords $this->db->order_by('column_name', 'RANDOM');.

Q: Disable ALL Auto Formatting on Save in VSCode A:

Struggled with issue as well: the VSCode level setting "Format On Save" is unchecked/disabled, but my .go files still got formatted on save.

My combination:

  • VSCode (cursor)

  • VIM extension

  • Go extension

My solution:

Add configs below in settings.json to disable Go extension's auto format behavior.

    "[go]": {
        "editor.formatOnSave": false
    }
